name: Cambridge
region: Greater Boston (inner core, across the Charles)
headline: Newtowne of 1630 on the Charles,
five Red Line stops and a reservoir to the west.
answer: Cambridge is a Middlesex County city of 118,403 people (2020 Census) on the north bank of the Charles River, across from Boston. Single-family homes are a small share of its housing: 6.4% of units, against 34.1% in buildings of more than 100 units, by the city's own count. The Warren Group recorded 105 single-family sales in 2025, a small market for a city of this size. Five Red Line stations run through Cambridge, from Alewife to Kendall/MIT, and Porter also has commuter rail.
overview: Cambridge was founded in December 1630 as Newtowne and renamed in May 1638 after the English university town, two years after the college that became Harvard was founded. George Washington took command of the Continental Army on Cambridge Common in 1775 and used the house at 105 Brattle Street as his first long-term headquarters during the siege of Boston. The West Boston Bridge of 1792 tied the town directly to Boston, and new bridges and roads turned estates and marshland into industrial and residential districts; the New England Glass Company, founded in 1818, with plants in what are now Kendall Square and East Cambridge, was the city's largest employer for much of the 19th century. Cambridge became a city in 1846. MIT moved here from Boston in 1916.

The city recognizes 13 neighborhoods on about 6.4 square miles of land. Squares strung along Massachusetts Avenue anchor them: Harvard Square beside the 22.4-acre Harvard Yard, where Massachusetts Hall has stood since 1720, Central Square with City Hall, and Porter Square farther north, while Kendall Square grew from salt marsh and 19th-century industry into an office and laboratory district beside MIT. Cambridgeport keeps streets of triple-deckers near the river. In the west, Fresh Pond Reservation surrounds the city's drinking-water reservoir, and Mount Auburn Cemetery, founded in 1831, straddles the line with Watertown. Danehy Park, a 50-acre former city dump in North Cambridge, opened as parkland in 1990.

On February 10, 2025, the City Council voted to allow multifamily housing citywide. Multifamily housing is now allowed in every zoning district except Open Space, and in the new base district, Residence C-1, residential buildings may rise to four stories (45 feet), or to six stories (74 feet) on lots of at least 5,000 square feet when 20 percent of the housing is income-restricted. Existing single-family homes may remain and new ones may still be built, and the city's inclusionary housing program continues. Since October 2020, the 100 Percent Affordable Housing Overlay, amended in 2023 and 2025, has allowed permanently affordable buildings denser than base zoning; completed projects include 52 New Street (106 rental units) and 116 Norfolk Street (62). The state lists Cambridge as compliant with the MBTA Communities law.

housing.text: By the city's inventory as of June 30, 2025, 6.4% of Cambridge's housing units are single-family homes, 11.9% are in two-unit buildings and 10.5% in three-unit buildings, while 34.1% are in buildings of more than 100 units. About two-thirds of occupied units (66.5%) are renter-occupied and 33.5% owner-occupied (2020 to 2024 American Community Survey). With so few single-family homes, The Warren Group's 105 single-family sales in 2025 reflect only a narrow part of the market.

villages.name: Harvard Square
villages.line: A triangular plaza where Massachusetts Avenue, Brattle Street and John F. Kennedy Street meet beside Harvard Yard, served by Harvard station on the Red Line and a bus hub.

villages.name: Central Square
villages.line: The seat of city government, centered where Massachusetts Avenue, Prospect Street and Western Avenue meet; a state-designated Cultural District since 2012, with Central station on the Red Line.

villages.name: Kendall Square
villages.line: Former Charles River salt marsh and industrial district where Main Street meets Broadway, named for the Kendall Boiler and Tank Company, now an office and lab district beside MIT with the Kendall/MIT Red Line stop.

villages.name: Cambridgeport
villages.line: A mostly residential neighborhood of triple-deckers between Massachusetts Avenue and the Charles River, with Magazine Beach and Fort Washington Park.

villages.name: East Cambridge
villages.line: The old Lechmere Point, once home to glassworks and factory cottages, between the Charles River, Somerville and Broadway, with Lechmere station relocated in 2022 for the Green Line Extension.

villages.name: Porter Square
villages.line: The square where Massachusetts Avenue meets Somerville Avenue, spanning Cambridge and Somerville, renamed in 1896 for Porter's Hotel and once lined with cattle yards; the Red Line reached Porter station in 1984, and it is also a Fitchburg Line commuter rail stop.

commute.text: Five Red Line stations serve Cambridge, from Alewife, which has a 2,471-space MBTA garage, through Porter, Harvard and Central to Kendall/MIT. Porter is also a Fitchburg Line commuter rail stop, about 15 minutes from Boston's North Station, and Lechmere in East Cambridge is on the Green Line. Route 2 enters at Alewife and runs with US 3 and Route 16 along Alewife Brook and Fresh Pond Parkways, then with US 3 along Memorial Drive beside the Charles.

places.name: Fresh Pond Reservation
places.line: 162 acres of open space around the 155-acre Fresh Pond reservoir, part of the city's drinking-water system, with nature walks and ranger programs.

places.name: Mount Auburn Cemetery
places.line: Established in 1831 between Cambridge and Watertown, a National Historic Landmark open to the public at no cost every day of the year.

places.name: Longfellow House-Washington's Headquarters
places.line: A National Historic Site at 105 Brattle Street, Washington's headquarters during the siege of Boston and later Henry Wadsworth Longfellow's home, with seasonal tours and a formal garden.

places.name: Cambridge Common
places.line: Public parkland where Washington took command of the Continental Army in 1775.

places.name: Harvard Yard
places.line: A 22.4-acre grassy enclosure bounded principally by Massachusetts Avenue, Cambridge Street, Broadway and Quincy Street, with Massachusetts Hall (1720), Harvard's oldest building, and Widener Library.

places.name: Danehy Park
places.line: A 50-acre North Cambridge park on a former brickyard and city dump, opened in 1990, with athletic fields, paths, a wetland area and the city's first Miyawaki forest, planted in 2021; the eastern entrance is at 99 Sherman Street.

places.name: MIT Museum
places.line: MIT's museum, founded in 1971, reopened on October 2, 2022 in the Gambrill Center at 314 Main Street in Kendall Square, beside the Kendall/MIT station; its collections include holography, robotics, architecture and the history of MIT.

places.name: Cambridge Public Library
places.line: The main library at 449 Broadway joins a Richardsonian Romanesque building of 1888 by Van Brunt & Howe with an expansion that opened on November 8, 2009; six neighborhood branches serve the rest of the city.

history.text: Founded in December 1630 as Newtowne; it was renamed Cambridge in May 1638.
The college that became Harvard was founded.
George Washington took command of the Patriot soldiers on Cambridge Common.
Cambridge was incorporated as a city.
MIT moved across the Charles River from Boston to its campus in Cambridge.

Residential exemption: 30%, which reduces the assessed value of an owner-occupied principal residence by $510,208 in FY2026 (City of Cambridge, FY26 Property Tax Update, https://www.cambridgema.gov/Departments/Finance/publications/2026/fy26propertytaxupdate). search_notes: 'Cambridge MA real estate agent' returns individual agent profiles on RE/MAX and Experience.com, HomeLight's top-agent list, a This Old House list and a headshot photographer's page. No result explains how small the city's single-family market is or how the squares, Red Line stops and neighborhoods fit together, which a sourced guide could cover.

faq.q: What is the median home price in Cambridge, MA?
faq.a: According to The Warren Group's MA December 2025 Sales, Prices by Town table, the median single-family sale price in Cambridge for calendar year 2025 was $2,175,000, across 105 sales. In 2024 it was $2,135,500, across 98 sales. Single-family homes are only 6.4% of the city's housing units, so these figures describe a small part of the market.

Yes. Porter is a stop on the MBTA Fitchburg Line, about 15 minutes from North Station. Cambridge also has five Red Line stations, Alewife, Porter, Harvard, Central and Kendall/MIT, and Lechmere on the Green Line.
Cambridge Public Schools. Review its profile with DESE.

faq.q: What is the property tax rate in Cambridge, MA?
faq.a: According to the Massachusetts Division of Local Services, Cambridge's FY2026 residential property tax rate is $6.67 per $1,000 of assessed value, and commercial, industrial and personal property pay $14.07. Owner-occupants who qualify for Cambridge's 30% residential exemption have $510,208 taken off their assessed value in FY2026, according to the City of Cambridge.

faq.q: What changed in Cambridge's zoning in 2025?
faq.a: On February 10, 2025, the City Council voted to allow multifamily housing in every district except Open Space. In the base Residence C-1 district, residential buildings may reach four stories (45 feet), or six stories (74 feet) on lots of at least 5,000 square feet when 20 percent of the housing is income-restricted. Single-family homes may still be kept or built.

notes: Condo fields null: the Warren PDF's extracted condo table is truncated at 'BROOKLI', before Cambridge. Wikipedia gives both July 2 and July 3, 1775 for Washington's arrival, so no day is used. The West Boston Bridge year differs between Wikipedia pages (1792 on Cambridge, 1793 on Kendall Square); the overview uses 1792 from the Cambridge page and a fact-checker may want to confirm. The city's structure-type shares come from the CDD inventory, which the city notes is not comparable to Census counts; the 66.5% renter figure is from the ACS on the same page. Kendall/MIT, Central, Harvard and Porter are listed as Cambridge Red Line stations on Wikipedia; Alewife's Cambridge address is from its MBTA stop page. The Porter travel time is read from the MBTA Fitchburg timetable. Mount Auburn acreage and 'first garden cemetery' claim were left out: its about page does not state them. Cambridge Common is sourced to Wikipedia only. Highways come from Wikipedia's Route 2 page. The 2016 city housing profile (7.2% single-family) was superseded by the 2025 figures used. Paragraph 1 adds the post-1792 growth of industrial and residential districts and the New England Glass Company (founded 1818, plants in what are now Kendall Square and East Cambridge, the city's largest employer for much of the 19th and early 20th centuries) from Cambridge Wikipedia. Paragraph 2 adds Harvard Yard (22.4 acres; Massachusetts Hall, 1720) from https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_Yard and Danehy Park (50 acres, former brickyard and city dump from 1952, opened 1990) from https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danehy_Park. New paragraph 3: the February 10, 2025 citywide multifamily vote, Residence C-1 base district, four stories (45 feet) or six stories (74 feet) on lots of 5,000 square feet or more with 20 percent income-restricted, all housing types allowed except in Open Space, single-family homes still allowed, inclusionary program unchanged (City of Cambridge CDD news, https://www.cambridgema.gov/CDD/News/2025/2/zoningformultifamilyhousingcitywide; the page says 20% of units in one place and 20% of residential floor area in its FAQ, so the copy says 'of the housing'); the 100 Percent Affordable Housing Overlay, adopted October 2020 and amended 2023 and 2025, with completed projects 52 New Street (106) and 116 Norfolk Street (62) (https://www.cambridgema.gov/cdd/housing/housingdevelopment/aho); Cambridge no. 25 on the state MBTA Communities compliance list as of October 21, 2026 (https://www.mass.gov/doc/mbta-communities-district-compliance-letters/download). Added village Porter Square (Wikipedia, renamed 1896, cattle yards, Red Line 1984); places Harvard Yard, Danehy Park, MIT Museum (founded 1971, reopened October 2, 2022 at 314 Main Street, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MIT_Museum) and Cambridge Public Library (449 Broadway, 1888 Van Brunt & Howe building, expansion opened November 8, 2009, six branches, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridge_Public_Library); history entry 1916 (MIT); FAQ on the 2025 zoning change. Left out: the city's own Danehy Park page and the DCR Magazine Beach page failed to load; Wikipedia's 'largest collection of holograms in the world' claim for the MIT Museum (superlative, not verified); September 2026 council proposals to adjust setbacks and limit heights for large units (WBUR, September 18, 2026, https://www.wbur.org/news/2026/09/18/cambridge-zoning-change), because the outcome of the expected September 28 vote was not confirmed; AHO pipeline unit totals, which the city page lists as planned rather than permitted. The CDD page does not use the phrase 'ended single-family zoning', which press coverage uses, so the copy does not either. Library 'built in 1888' per Wikipedia (some sources say 1889). Market figures unchanged. Fact-check 2026-10-22 (deepening): verified with WebFetch against the City of Cambridge CDD page 'Cambridge Zones for Multifamily Housing Citywide': the February 10, 2025 vote; 'all districts (except open space) are zoned to allow multifamily housing'; Residence A-1, A-2, B and C are now Residence C-1, described as new base zoning for most neighborhoods; residential developments up to four stories (45 feet), or six stories (74 feet) with a lot of at least 5,000 square feet and 20 percent affordable; existing single-family homes can remain and new ones can be built; inclusionary requirements unchanged. The page is internally inconsistent on the six-story conditions (highlights: 20% of units and a lot of 'at least' 5,000 square feet; FAQ: 20% of residential floor area and a lot 'over' 5,000 square feet), so 'at least' and 'of the housing' were kept and the ordinance text controls. Also verified: AHO adopted October 2020 and amended 2023 and 2025, denser than base zoning, 52 New Street (106 rental units) and 116 Norfolk Street (62) (city AHO page); Cambridge no. 25 on the state compliance list as of October 21, 2026; West Boston Bridge 1792, the estates-and-marshland sentence, New England Glass Company (1818, Kendall Square and East Cambridge, largest employer) and MIT's 1916 move (Cambridge Wikipedia); Harvard Yard 22.4 acres, 'grassy', its four bounding streets, Massachusetts Hall (1720) as 'Harvard's oldest building', Widener (Harvard Yard Wikipedia); Danehy Park 50 acres, brickyard and dump from 1952, opened 1990, fields, paths, wetland, Cambridge's first Miyawaki forest (September 2021), eastern entrance 99 Sherman Street; MIT Museum 1971, reopened October 2, 2022, Gambrill Center at 314 Main Street beside the Kendall/MIT headhouse, collections; Cambridge Public Library 449 Broadway, 1888, Richardsonian Romanesque by Van Brunt & Howe, expansion opened November 8, 2009, six branches; Porter Square renamed 1896 after Porter's Hotel, cattle yards, Red Line extended through Porter in 1984, Fitchburg Line stop. Corrected: 'All housing types are now permitted in every zoning district except Open Space' now reads 'Multifamily housing is now allowed', the city's wording (its 'all types of housing' line is about Residence C-1 only); Porter Square 'on the Somerville line' now reads 'spanning Cambridge and Somerville', as its source says; Harvard Yard is 'bounded principally by' its four streets, as the source qualifies. Removed: nothing. Still unconfirmed: the CDD page carries a dated-information warning, and WBUR (September 18, 2026) reported proposed amendments (larger setbacks and a three-story limit for buildings with large units) with a council vote expected September 28, 2026; the outcome was not found, so the C-1 height rules are stated as adopted in February 2025 and should be rechecked against the current Zoning Ordinance before launch.
